title: Legume Pod Borer: How to Spot It and Protect Your Sitaw and Beans
metaTitle: Legume Pod Borer: Signs, Damage and Control
metaDescription: The legume pod borer eats the flowers and seeds of sitaw, cowpea and mungbean from the inside. Learn the signs and how to control it step by step.
excerpt: The legume pod borer is a moth caterpillar that webs flowers together and bores into the pods of sitaw, cowpea, pigeon pea and mungbean. It eats the seeds from the inside, where sprays hardly reach. This page shows how to spot the legume pod borer early and how to cut the loss.

heroImage.alt: An adult legume pod borer moth, Maruca vitrata, brown with white patches on its wings
heroImage.credit: Kai Squires, CC BY, via iNaturalist

blocks.text:
The legume pod borer (Maruca vitrata) is also called the bean pod borer. It lives in the tropics worldwide, including Asia. Many legumes host it, such as French bean, cowpea, pigeon pea, yardlong bean and mungbean.

It counts as a major pest. The caterpillars tunnel into the pods and feed on the seeds, so what you harvest is empty or spoiled. Because they hide inside flowers and pods, the damage often shows only when it is too late for a spray to help.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Sitaw (yardlong bean), string bean, cowpea, pigeon pea, mungbean and other legumes
It attacks from flowering to pod filling, and the young caterpillars hide in the flowers before they move into the pods.

The moth lays pale eggs one by one on stems, young leaves, flowers and pods. For about a week the young caterpillars eat inside the flowers, and then they tunnel into the pods. When they reach 18 mm, they leave the pod and pupate in the soil.

blocks.text: How to Identify Legume Pod Borer

Look at the flowers first. Damaged flowers, and leaves, buds and pods tied together with fine webbing, are the early sign. Then check the pods for small entry holes with frass, which is the chewed remains and droppings, around them. Open a pod and you will find a caterpillar of up to 18 mm. The adult moth has brown front wings with white patches and mostly white hind wings edged with brown. A related pest, the [bean fly](/pests/bean-fly), attacks only seedlings, not the pods.

items: Flowers that are chewed, webbed together or dropping.
Leaves, buds and pods tied together with fine silk.
Small entry holes in the pods with frass around them.
Seeds eaten out and pods that rot inside.
Caterpillars up to 18 mm long inside flowers and pods.
Frass, the chewed remains and droppings, around the entry holes and on the pods.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: The [bean fly](/pests/bean-fly) also attacks legumes, but it hits seedlings in the first 3 to 4 weeks. This pest attacks the flowers and pods.
How Legume Pod Borer Hurts Your Crop

The caterpillars cause the main loss by eating the seeds, according to the Pacific Pests fact sheet. The webbing damage on buds, flowers and leaves is minor next to the pod damage.

We found no Philippine yield loss figure or action threshold in the sources we could open. The sheet does say that sprays often disappoint, because the caterpillars hide, the cost is high, the natural enemies die and resistance builds up. So the best plan is to check the flowers every few days and remove infested parts early.

In one cowpea trial in India, a sequence of three sprays from 50 percent flowering, at 10 day intervals, cut pod damage to about 12 percent and gave about 66 percent protection over the untreated plots. That is one trial, so your result may differ. A study in Burkina Faso found that the larvae prefer the reproductive parts of the flowers, which is why early checks at flowering matter.
How to Control Legume Pod Borer

items: Check the flowers and the young pods every two or three days once the plants begin to flower. Look for webbing and for caterpillars inside the flowers, which are where the larvae feed first.
Handpick the caterpillars and the webbed flowers early, when the infestation is still small, and destroy them.
Do not plant sitaw or beans next to a field that is already infested. Avoid planting legume after legume in the same plot.
Plant the beans in rows between rows of maize or sorghum. The Pacific Pests fact sheet says this intercropping works in Africa, so test it on a small part of your field first.
After harvest, destroy all crop remains, so the pupae and the remaining caterpillars do not feed the next generation.

Plant tolerant varieties when they are sold for your area, and keep the broad spectrum sprays away from the field, so the natural enemies stay. See the [integrated pest management guide](/pests/integrated-pest-management).

blocks.text: Pacific Pests discourages routine spraying, because the caterpillars hide, sprays kill natural enemies and resistance builds up. If you must spray, use plant based or biological products first. Time the spray at flowering, when the young caterpillars still feed in the flowers, and follow the FPA registered label and the waiting time before harvest. An Indian trial rotated three different groups at 10 day intervals from half flowering, which also helps slow resistance.

**Resistance.** Pod borer in parts of Asia already survives some pyrethroids and organophosphates. Keep one group per window and switch: a diamide (28), then spinosad (5), then indoxacarb (22A) or emamectin (6).

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different insecticide group next time, so the pest does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to integrated pest management](/pests/integrated-pest-management) explains how.

items: From first bloom, check flowers and young pods every 2 to 3 days and pick off webbed flowers and larvae by hand.
Do not plant beans beside an infested field, and avoid legume after legume in the same plot.
Rows of corn or sorghum between bean rows can cut borer attack. Try it on a small plot first.
Pick pods often. Old pods left on the vine breed more borers.
Destroy crop remains right after harvest, so pupae and larvae do not feed the next generation.
Grow tolerant varieties where they are sold for your area.
Small wasps, spiders and earwigs attack the larvae. Broad sprays kill them and the borer returns.
Bt and neem sprayed at flowering reach young larvae in the flowers before they enter the pods.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Legume Pod Borer

items.q: Why are my sitaw pods rotten and empty inside?
items.a: The legume pod borer is a likely cause. The caterpillar bores into the pod and eats the seeds. Open a few pods and look for the caterpillar and its frass.

items.q: When should I check for the legume pod borer?
items.a: Begin when the first flowers open. The young caterpillars feed in the flowers for about a week before they move into the pods, so this is the best time to find and remove them.

items.q: Why does spraying not stop the damage?
items.a: The caterpillars feed inside flowers and pods where the spray cannot reach. Sprays can also kill the natural enemies. That is why removing infested parts and cleaning the field matter more.
